newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium to split ASLK-CGER between bourse, Fortis.
newsitem.headline: Belgium to split ASLK-CGER between bourse, Fortis.

text.p: The Belgian government said on Friday it would sell-off a further 24.7 percent of banking and insurance group ASLK-CGER, with shares going to Dutch-Belgian financial group Fortis and the rest to the Brussels bourse.

Fortis, owned jointly by Fortis AG and Fortis AMEV , which bought 49.9 percent of ASLK-CGER in 1993 for 35 billion Belgian francs ($924 million), will pay at least eight billion francs for an additional 9.8 percent, Belgian finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told a news conference.
But the final price would be based on the amount raised from an initial public offering (IPO) of 14.9 percent in the autumn.
"The price Fortis pays cannot be less than the price set during the bourse listing," Maystadt, speaking after the government's last cabinet meeting before the summer, said.
Fortis and the government agreed an eight billion franc price-tag at the time of the original privatisation. Maystadt said, however, it had now been renegotiated.

"If we applied the 1993 agreement (the price) would be about eight billion Belgian francs. It will be more because ASLK-CGER has since increased in value and the stock market has risen greatly," Maystadt said.
The details and timing of the bourse listing were not yet fixed.

Maystadt said that before the listing could take place, Belgium had to formally change laws governing ASLK-CGER's public ownership, allowing the group - presently two separate banking and insurance companies -- to be restructured.
After the restructuring, ASLK-CGER Insurance would become a subsidiary of the listed ASLK-CGER Bank.
The Belgian state holding company SFP/FPM had not yet appointed issue managers to coordinate the offering, he added.
Belgium plans to use the money raised from the sale and bourse listing to re-pay part of its huge debt, Maystadt said.

Belgium has set itself a target of reducing its debt to 127 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 1997. Maystadt said, however, that because 1997's public finances were turning out better than expected not all the ASLK-CGER sale funds would be needed to meet that goal. "It could be used (in 1998)," he said.
The Belgian government said earlier on Friday it was confident of reducing its public deficit to 2.8 percent of GDP in 1997, below a target of 2.9 percent set last October.
